messages.content: You are an agent playing a game. Select the action that maximizes your probability of winning.

You are playing a game called Santorini. The rules are as follows:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

- Game: Santorini

- Solution concept: minimax-style best response with tactical win, block, and mobility evaluation

Reasoning workflow
- Check for a legal immediate win by moving to level 3.
- If no immediate win, block the opponent's immediate level-3 threats.
- Choose move-build pairs that improve own height access and reduce opponent mobility.
- Verify the move and build are both legal in the listed action id.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. Choose the legal action that best advances your chance of winning.

You are a precise strategic game agent. Return valid JSON only.

You are a strategic game-playing agent using high_reasoning engineered field reasoning.

Game: Santorini
Strategic style: board_tactics

Engineered field reasoning:
Prompt variant: high_reasoning
You are executing an engineered field reasoning prompt built from game rules and game theory.
The field register below is fixed by the experiment. Do not invent or redefine fields; compute their current values from the observation, then reason over those fields to choose a legal action.
Unlike high_distill, this variant does not give an executable decision program. The model must use the computed fields to compare candidate legal actions.

Game-theoretic frame
- Game: Santorini
- Model: two-player deterministic spatial game with move-build turns and immediate win conditions
- Solution concept: minimax-style best response with tactical win, block, and mobility evaluation
- Mapping: Model each turn as a move followed by a build. Legal actions are constrained by adjacency, height difference, occupancy, and domes. Payoff is immediate win by moving to level 3 or forcing opponent immobility.

Reference basis
- GameBench paper Appendix F/G: Santorini description and rules
- GameBench implementation: games/santorini/santorini.py
- Santorini rulebook: games/santorini/rulebook.pdf
- Game theory: finite extensive game with perfect information, backward-induction-style tactical search, and maxmin defense

Field register: base fields
- current_phase_placement_or_move_build
- active_pawn
- board_heights_and_occupancy
- legal_action_set
- active_phase_specific_field_set

Field register: role or phase-specific fields
- Selection rule: If the observation is placing pawns or legal actions are board coordinates before movement, use placement_phase. If the action ids encode move/build pairs or the observation describes a current pawn turn, use move_build_phase.
- placement_phase:
  - own_unplaced_pawn
  - empty_board_squares
  - centrality_and_future_mobility_value
  - pair_spacing_between_own_pawns
  - opponent_placement_pressure
  - candidate_placement_values
- move_build_phase:
  - legal_move_squares
  - legal_build_squares_after_move
  - immediate_win_moves
  - opponent_immediate_win_threats
  - mobility_after_action
  - height_access_to_level_three
  - candidate_move_build_values

Reasoning workflow
- Check for a legal immediate win by moving to level 3.
- If no immediate win, block the opponent's immediate level-3 threats.
- Choose move-build pairs that improve own height access and reduce opponent mobility.
- Verify the move and build are both legal in the listed action id.

Verifier checks
- move is adjacent and does not climb more than one level
- build is adjacent to the moved pawn and on an unoccupied non-dome square
- selected_action is exactly listed

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

You are executing an engineered field reasoning prompt built from game rules and game theory.

- Solution concept: minimax-style best response with tactical win, block, and mobility evaluation
- Mapping: Model each turn as a move followed by a build. Legal actions are constrained by adjacency, height difference, occupancy, and domes. Payoff is immediate win by moving to level 3 or forcing opponent immobility.

- GameBench implementation: games/santorini/santorini.py

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. Choose the legal action that best advances your chance of winning.

You are a strategic game-playing agent using high_reasoning engineered field reasoning.

Game: Santorini
Strategic style: board_tactics

Engineered field reasoning:
Prompt variant: high_reasoning
You are executing an engineered field reasoning prompt built from game rules and game theory.
The field register below is fixed by the experiment. Do not invent or redefine fields; compute their current values from the observation, then reason over those fields to choose a legal action.
Unlike high_distill, this variant does not give an executable decision program. The model must use the computed fields to compare candidate legal actions.

Game-theoretic frame
- Game: Santorini
- Model: two-player deterministic spatial game with move-build turns and immediate win conditions
- Solution concept: minimax-style best response with tactical win, block, and mobility evaluation
- Mapping: Model each turn as a move followed by a build. Legal actions are constrained by adjacency, height difference, occupancy, and domes. Payoff is immediate win by moving to level 3 or forcing opponent immobility.

Reference basis
- GameBench paper Appendix F/G: Santorini description and rules
- GameBench implementation: games/santorini/santorini.py
- Santorini rulebook: games/santorini/rulebook.pdf
- Game theory: finite extensive game with perfect information, backward-induction-style tactical search, and maxmin defense

Field register: base fields
- current_phase_placement_or_move_build
- active_pawn
- board_heights_and_occupancy
- legal_action_set
- active_phase_specific_field_set

Field register: role or phase-specific fields
- Selection rule: If the observation is placing pawns or legal actions are board coordinates before movement, use placement_phase. If the action ids encode move/build pairs or the observation describes a current pawn turn, use move_build_phase.
- placement_phase:
  - own_unplaced_pawn
  - empty_board_squares
  - centrality_and_future_mobility_value
  - pair_spacing_between_own_pawns
  - opponent_placement_pressure
  - candidate_placement_values
- move_build_phase:
  - legal_move_squares
  - legal_build_squares_after_move
  - immediate_win_moves
  - opponent_immediate_win_threats
  - mobility_after_action
  - height_access_to_level_three
  - candidate_move_build_values

Reasoning workflow
- Check for a legal immediate win by moving to level 3.
- If no immediate win, block the opponent's immediate level-3 threats.
- Choose move-build pairs that improve own height access and reduce opponent mobility.
- Verify the move and build are both legal in the listed action id.

Verifier checks
- move is adjacent and does not climb more than one level
- build is adjacent to the moved pawn and on an unoccupied non-dome square
- selected_action is exactly listed

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Choose the legal action that best advances your chance of winning.

Prompt variant: high_reasoning
You are executing an engineered field reasoning prompt built from game rules and game theory.
The field register below is fixed by the experiment. Do not invent or redefine fields; compute their current values from the observation, then reason over those fields to choose a legal action.
Unlike high_distill, this variant does not give an executable decision program. The model must use the computed fields to compare candidate legal actions.

Game-theoretic frame
- Game: Santorini
- Model: two-player deterministic spatial game with move-build turns and immediate win conditions
- Solution concept: minimax-style best response with tactical win, block, and mobility evaluation
- Mapping: Model each turn as a move followed by a build. Legal actions are constrained by adjacency, height difference, occupancy, and domes. Payoff is immediate win by moving to level 3 or forcing opponent immobility.

Reference basis
- GameBench paper Appendix F/G: Santorini description and rules
- GameBench implementation: games/santorini/santorini.py
- Santorini rulebook: games/santorini/rulebook.pdf
- Game theory: finite extensive game with perfect information, backward-induction-style tactical search, and maxmin defense

- current_phase_placement_or_move_build
- active_pawn
- board_heights_and_occupancy
- legal_action_set
- active_phase_specific_field_set

Field register: role or phase-specific fields
- Selection rule: If the observation is placing pawns or legal actions are board coordinates before movement, use placement_phase. If the action ids encode move/build pairs or the observation describes a current pawn turn, use move_build_phase.
- placement_phase:
  - own_unplaced_pawn
  - empty_board_squares
  - centrality_and_future_mobility_value
  - pair_spacing_between_own_pawns
  - opponent_placement_pressure
  - candidate_placement_values
- move_build_phase:
  - legal_move_squares
  - legal_build_squares_after_move
  - immediate_win_moves
  - opponent_immediate_win_threats
  - mobility_after_action
  - height_access_to_level_three
  - candidate_move_build_values

Reasoning workflow
- Check for a legal immediate win by moving to level 3.
- If no immediate win, block the opponent's immediate level-3 threats.
- Choose move-build pairs that improve own height access and reduce opponent mobility.
- Verify the move and build are both legal in the listed action id.

Verifier checks
- move is adjacent and does not climb more than one level
- build is adjacent to the moved pawn and on an unoccupied non-dome square
- selected_action is exactly listed

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Reasoning workflow

- If no immediate win, block the opponent's immediate level-3 threats.
- Choose move-build pairs that improve own height access and reduce opponent mobility.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Prompt variant: high_reasoning
You are executing an engineered field reasoning prompt built from game rules and game theory.
The field register below is fixed by the experiment. Do not invent or redefine fields; compute their current values from the observation, then reason over those fields to choose a legal action.

Game-theoretic frame
- Game: Santorini
- Model: two-player deterministic spatial game with move-build turns and immediate win conditions
- Solution concept: minimax-style best response with tactical win, block, and mobility evaluation
- Mapping: Model each turn as a move followed by a build. Legal actions are constrained by adjacency, height difference, occupancy, and domes. Payoff is immediate win by moving to level 3 or forcing opponent immobility.

Reference basis

- GameBench implementation: games/santorini/santorini.py
- Santorini rulebook: games/santorini/rulebook.pdf
- Game theory: finite extensive game with perfect information, backward-induction-style tactical search, and maxmin defense

Field register: role or phase-specific fields

- placement_phase:

  - mobility_after_action
  - height_access_to_level_three

Reasoning workflow
- Check for a legal immediate win by moving to level 3.
- If no immediate win, block the opponent's immediate level-3 threats.
- Choose move-build pairs that improve own height access and reduce opponent mobility.
- Verify the move and build are both legal in the listed action id.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

The field register below is fixed by the experiment. Do not invent or redefine fields; compute their current values from the observation, then reason over those fields to choose a legal action.
Unlike high_distill, this variant does not give an executable decision program. The model must use the computed fields to compare candidate legal actions.

Game-theoretic frame
- Game: Santorini
- Model: two-player deterministic spatial game with move-build turns and immediate win conditions
- Solution concept: minimax-style best response with tactical win, block, and mobility evaluation
- Mapping: Model each turn as a move followed by a build. Legal actions are constrained by adjacency, height difference, occupancy, and domes. Payoff is immediate win by moving to level 3 or forcing opponent immobility.

- Santorini rulebook: games/santorini/rulebook.pdf
- Game theory: finite extensive game with perfect information, backward-induction-style tactical search, and maxmin defense

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Prompt variant: high_reasoning
You are executing an engineered field reasoning prompt built from game rules and game theory.
The field register below is fixed by the experiment. Do not invent or redefine fields; compute their current values from the observation, then reason over those fields to choose a legal action.
Unlike high_distill, this variant does not give an executable decision program. The model must use the computed fields to compare candidate legal actions.

Game-theoretic frame
- Game: Santorini
- Model: two-player deterministic spatial game with move-build turns and immediate win conditions
- Solution concept: minimax-style best response with tactical win, block, and mobility evaluation
- Mapping: Model each turn as a move followed by a build. Legal actions are constrained by adjacency, height difference, occupancy, and domes. Payoff is immediate win by moving to level 3 or forcing opponent immobility.

Reference basis
- GameBench paper Appendix F/G: Santorini description and rules
- GameBench implementation: games/santorini/santorini.py
- Santorini rulebook: games/santorini/rulebook.pdf
- Game theory: finite extensive game with perfect information, backward-induction-style tactical search, and maxmin defense

- Check for a legal immediate win by moving to level 3.
- If no immediate win, block the opponent's immediate level-3 threats.

- Verify the move and build are both legal in the listed action id.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

You are executing an engineered field reasoning prompt built from game rules and game theory.
The field register below is fixed by the experiment. Do not invent or redefine fields; compute their current values from the observation, then reason over those fields to choose a legal action.

- Game: Santorini

- Solution concept: minimax-style best response with tactical win, block, and mobility evaluation
- Mapping: Model each turn as a move followed by a build. Legal actions are constrained by adjacency, height difference, occupancy, and domes. Payoff is immediate win by moving to level 3 or forcing opponent immobility.

Reference basis

- GameBench implementation: games/santorini/santorini.py
- Santorini rulebook: games/santorini/rulebook.pdf
- Game theory: finite extensive game with perfect information, backward-induction-style tactical search, and maxmin defense

Reasoning workflow
- Check for a legal immediate win by moving to level 3.
- If no immediate win, block the opponent's immediate level-3 threats.
- Choose move-build pairs that improve own height access and reduce opponent mobility.
- Verify the move and build are both legal in the listed action id.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Choose the legal action that best advances your chance of winning.

You are a strategic game-playing agent using high_reasoning engineered field reasoning.

Game: Santorini
Strategic style: board_tactics

Engineered field reasoning:
Prompt variant: high_reasoning
You are executing an engineered field reasoning prompt built from game rules and game theory.
The field register below is fixed by the experiment. Do not invent or redefine fields; compute their current values from the observation, then reason over those fields to choose a legal action.
Unlike high_distill, this variant does not give an executable decision program. The model must use the computed fields to compare candidate legal actions.

Game-theoretic frame
- Game: Santorini
- Model: two-player deterministic spatial game with move-build turns and immediate win conditions
- Solution concept: minimax-style best response with tactical win, block, and mobility evaluation
- Mapping: Model each turn as a move followed by a build. Legal actions are constrained by adjacency, height difference, occupancy, and domes. Payoff is immediate win by moving to level 3 or forcing opponent immobility.

Reference basis
- GameBench paper Appendix F/G: Santorini description and rules
- GameBench implementation: games/santorini/santorini.py
- Santorini rulebook: games/santorini/rulebook.pdf
- Game theory: finite extensive game with perfect information, backward-induction-style tactical search, and maxmin defense

Field register: base fields
- current_phase_placement_or_move_build
- active_pawn
- board_heights_and_occupancy
- legal_action_set
- active_phase_specific_field_set

Field register: role or phase-specific fields
- Selection rule: If the observation is placing pawns or legal actions are board coordinates before movement, use placement_phase. If the action ids encode move/build pairs or the observation describes a current pawn turn, use move_build_phase.
- placement_phase:
  - own_unplaced_pawn
  - empty_board_squares
  - centrality_and_future_mobility_value
  - pair_spacing_between_own_pawns
  - opponent_placement_pressure
  - candidate_placement_values
- move_build_phase:
  - legal_move_squares
  - legal_build_squares_after_move
  - immediate_win_moves
  - opponent_immediate_win_threats
  - mobility_after_action
  - height_access_to_level_three
  - candidate_move_build_values

Reasoning workflow
- Check for a legal immediate win by moving to level 3.
- If no immediate win, block the opponent's immediate level-3 threats.
- Choose move-build pairs that improve own height access and reduce opponent mobility.
- Verify the move and build are both legal in the listed action id.

Verifier checks
- move is adjacent and does not climb more than one level
- build is adjacent to the moved pawn and on an unoccupied non-dome square
- selected_action is exactly listed

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). Choose the legal action that best advances your chance of winning.

You are a precise strategic game agent. Return valid JSON only.

You are a strategic game-playing agent using high_reasoning engineered field reasoning.

Game: Santorini
Strategic style: board_tactics

Engineered field reasoning:
Prompt variant: high_reasoning
You are executing an engineered field reasoning prompt built from game rules and game theory.
The field register below is fixed by the experiment. Do not invent or redefine fields; compute their current values from the observation, then reason over those fields to choose a legal action.
Unlike high_distill, this variant does not give an executable decision program. The model must use the computed fields to compare candidate legal actions.

Game-theoretic frame
- Game: Santorini
- Model: two-player deterministic spatial game with move-build turns and immediate win conditions
- Solution concept: minimax-style best response with tactical win, block, and mobility evaluation
- Mapping: Model each turn as a move followed by a build. Legal actions are constrained by adjacency, height difference, occupancy, and domes. Payoff is immediate win by moving to level 3 or forcing opponent immobility.

Reference basis
- GameBench paper Appendix F/G: Santorini description and rules
- GameBench implementation: games/santorini/santorini.py
- Santorini rulebook: games/santorini/rulebook.pdf
- Game theory: finite extensive game with perfect information, backward-induction-style tactical search, and maxmin defense

Field register: base fields
- current_phase_placement_or_move_build
- active_pawn
- board_heights_and_occupancy
- legal_action_set
- active_phase_specific_field_set

Field register: role or phase-specific fields
- Selection rule: If the observation is placing pawns or legal actions are board coordinates before movement, use placement_phase. If the action ids encode move/build pairs or the observation describes a current pawn turn, use move_build_phase.
- placement_phase:
  - own_unplaced_pawn
  - empty_board_squares
  - centrality_and_future_mobility_value
  - pair_spacing_between_own_pawns
  - opponent_placement_pressure
  - candidate_placement_values
- move_build_phase:
  - legal_move_squares
  - legal_build_squares_after_move
  - immediate_win_moves
  - opponent_immediate_win_threats
  - mobility_after_action
  - height_access_to_level_three
  - candidate_move_build_values

Reasoning workflow
- Check for a legal immediate win by moving to level 3.
- If no immediate win, block the opponent's immediate level-3 threats.
- Choose move-build pairs that improve own height access and reduce opponent mobility.
- Verify the move and build are both legal in the listed action id.

Verifier checks
- move is adjacent and does not climb more than one level
- build is adjacent to the moved pawn and on an unoccupied non-dome square
- selected_action is exactly listed

Rules summary:
Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). They cannot move their pawn onto a square that is occupied by another pawn, more than one level higher than the pawn, or at level 4. They can move a pawn any number of levels down, to the same level, or one level higher, but not more than one level higher and not to level 4.

During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it. They can place a block onto an unoccupied square at any level less than 4. Once a square has been built to level 4, it is "complete", meaning pawns cannot move to it and blocks cannot be placed on it. The player instantly wins if they move their pawn onto a square at level 3 or if they force their opponent to not be able to finish their turn.

Win by moving one of your pawns to the third level of the board or forcing your opponent to be unable to finish their turn. The game is played on a five by five grid of squares, and each player controls two pawns. Play alternates between the players, starting with player 1. The pawn that a player plays with alternates during each of their turns: for example, player 1 plays pawn A on their first turn, pawn B on their next turn, then pawn A, and so on. Blocks can be placed on squares on the board up to four blocks high, creating four possible height levels.

The board begins with no blocks placed, so every square begins at level 0. Before the game starts, each of the players takes turns placing each of their pawns on the board. A square is occupied if a pawn is on it.

Each turn consists of two stages: the "move" stage and the "build" stage. During the move stage, the player moves their pawn by one square (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally). During the build stage, the player must select an unoccupied square adjacent to the pawn they moved during the move stage and place a block on it.
